toc.title: Inspect and Adapt at Each Event (CSM 1.7)
Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

html:
1The Events in Scrum

"The Sprint is a container for all other events. Each event in Scrum is a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt Scrum artifacts. These events are specifically designed to enable the transparency required."

  • "Failure to operate any events as prescribed results in lost opportunities to inspect and adapt."
  • Events "are used in Scrum to create regularity and to minimize the need for meetings not defined in Scrum."
  • "Optimally, all events are held at the same time and place to reduce complexity."

There are five events: the Sprint and the four events inside it.

1.1 The four events inside the Sprint (SF 3.4)

Event Purpose Participants Maximum timebox (one-month Sprint) Place in the sequence
Sprint Planning Initiates the Sprint by laying out the work to be performed; the plan is created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team The Scrum Team; others may be invited to give advice 8 hours First event; starts the Sprint
Daily Scrum Inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog, adjusting the upcoming planned work The Developers (the Product Owner or Scrum Master only if working on Sprint Backlog items) 15 minutes Every working day of the Sprint
Sprint Review Inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations The Scrum Team and key stakeholders 4 hours Second to last event of the Sprint
Sprint Retrospective Plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness The Scrum Team 3 hours Concludes the Sprint

For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter (the Guide says this for Planning, Review and Retrospective). The Daily Scrum is 15 minutes whatever the Sprint length.

Exam angle

memorize 8 hours, 15 minutes, 4 hours, 3 hours for a one-month Sprint, and the sequence Planning → Daily Scrums (with the work) → Review → Retrospective. These are maximum timeboxes: an event may be shorter, never longer.

Old wording

The same four timeboxes were in the 2017 Guide (eight hours, 15 minutes, four hours, three hours). Common practice calls the events "ceremonies" or "meetings"; the Guide says events. Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity, not one of the five events.

2The Sprint (SF 3.2)

"Sprints are the heartbeat of Scrum, where ideas are turned into value."

Feature Guide wording
Length Fixed length events of one month or less to create consistency
Start of the next "A new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint"
What happens inside "All the work necessary to achieve the Product Goal, including Sprint Planning, Daily Scrums, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective, happen within Sprints"
Purpose Turn ideas into value; enable predictability by ensuring inspection and adaptation of progress toward a Product Goal at least every calendar month
View "Each Sprint may be considered a short project"

2.1 During the Sprint

Rule Meaning
No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal The goal is stable; the plan can change (Topic 11)
Quality does not decrease The Definition of Done is not lowered to save time
The Product Backlog is refined as needed Refinement goes on during the Sprint (Topic 10)
Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned The Developers and the Product Owner talk, without changing the goal

Not in Scrum (inferred from the rules above) Beyond the Guide: extending a Sprint when the team is late, shortening it because work is done early, a "Sprint 0" before the real Sprints, a "hardening" or "release" Sprint, or a gap between Sprints. All necessary work happens inside Sprints and the next Sprint starts immediately.

2.2 Forecasting practices

Burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flows are "proven useful" but "do not replace the importance of empiricism." In complex environments, "only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making."

3Timeboxes (SF 3.1)

A timebox is a fixed maximum duration. The Guide times every event ("timeboxed to a maximum of") and makes Sprints fixed length.

3.1 Benefits (list at least three) Beyond the Guide

Benefit Why
Regularity and predictability The team and stakeholders know when events happen: the Guide says events "create regularity"
Focus A fixed limit keeps discussion on what matters and prevents endless meetings or analysis
Faster decisions A deadline forces the group to decide and move on
Limits waste and risk A Sprint limits cost and effort to a short time frame; a wrong direction is found early
A regular rhythm of inspection and adaptation Each timebox ends with a chance to look at the result and change
Fewer unplanned meetings The events replace many extra meetings
Protects the team Work is not endlessly extended, which supports a sustainable pace

4Choosing a Sprint Length (SF 3.3)

The Guide sets the boundary: one month or less. It gives the reasoning for the choice:

  • "When a Sprint's horizon is too long the Sprint Goal may become invalid, complexity may rise, and risk may increase."
  • "Shorter Sprints can be employed to generate more learning cycles and limit risk of cost and effort to a smaller time frame."

4.1 Factors to weigh Beyond the Guide

Factor Points to
How fast feedback is needed, and how fast the market or needs change Shorter Sprints
How uncertain or risky the work is Shorter Sprints, so the team learns sooner
How long a usable Increment takes (build, test, deploy, dependencies, regulation) A length in which the Definition of Done can be met
Stakeholder availability A length that lets stakeholders attend the Review
Event overhead Very short Sprints mean the same events more often
Team experience New teams often start longer and shorten as they learn

Rule of thumb: pick the shortest length in which the team can regularly finish a usable Increment, keep it fixed so that it creates consistency, and revisit it with the team. The Guide does not name a preferred length: "two weeks" is a popular practice, not a rule.

Exam angle

answers expressing a Sprint longer than one month are wrong. When the question stresses uncertainty, fast change or risk, the best answer is shorter Sprints. The Sprint length is fixed: it does not stretch to finish work.

5Inspect and Adapt at Each Event (CSM 1.7)

The learning objective asks for at least one example of inspecting and adapting, to increase transparency, at each event. Examples Beyond the Guide built on the Guide's purposes:

Event What is inspected Example of adaptation Transparency gained
Sprint Planning The Product Backlog, the Product Goal, past performance, capacity and the Definition of Done The team forms a Sprint Goal and selects only the items that fit Everyone sees the Sprint Goal and the Sprint Backlog
Daily Scrum Progress toward the Sprint Goal The Developers reorder tasks or change who works on what for the next day The Sprint Backlog is current and shows real progress and impediments
Sprint Review The Increment and what has changed in the environment The Product Owner reorders or adds Product Backlog items Stakeholders and the team share the same view of the product and its progress
Sprint Retrospective How the last Sprint went: individuals, interactions, processes, tools and the Definition of Done The team adds its most helpful improvement to the next Sprint Backlog Problems and their causes are discussed in the open
The Sprint (the whole) Progress toward the Product Goal, at least every calendar month The Product Goal path is adjusted The state of the product is visible every Sprint

6Cancelling a Sprint (CSM 1.14)

"A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint."

Question Answer
When Only when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete (the objective no longer makes sense, for example because the organization changes direction or the market or technology changes) Beyond the Guideexamples
Who Only the Product Owner. The Scrum Master, the Developers and stakeholders may raise the concern
Not a reason The work is harder than expected, the team is behind, a Developer leaves, a manager wants something else, or time is running out. In those cases the Developers and the Product Owner negotiate scope without affecting the Sprint Goal
Old wording

The 2017 Guide had a longer section on cancelling. The Product Owner could cancel "under influence from the stakeholders, the Development Team, or the Scrum Master". Completed "Done" items were reviewed and may be accepted. Incomplete items were "re-estimated and put back on the Product Backlog". Cancellations "are often traumatic to the Scrum Team, and are very uncommon". The 2020 Guide kept only the condition and the authority.

7Events Compared

Planning Daily Scrum Review Retrospective
Looks at Product Backlog and capacity Progress toward the Sprint Goal The Increment and the environment The way of working
Outcome Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog An actionable plan for the next day of work Adjusted Product Backlog; next steps Improvements, perhaps in the next Sprint Backlog
Who Scrum Team (others for advice) Developers Scrum Team and key stakeholders Scrum Team
Maximum (one month) 8 h 15 min 4 h 3 h

8Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

  1. Fixed length, one month or less. Never longer, never stretched to finish, never cut short because "we are done".
  2. A new Sprint starts immediately. There is no break, no Sprint 0, no hardening or release Sprint.
  3. Events are maximum timeboxes, 8 hours, 15 minutes, 4 hours and 3 hours for a one-month Sprint. The Daily Scrum is always 15 minutes.
  4. The Review is the second to last event; the Retrospective concludes the Sprint.
  5. Skipping an event loses an opportunity to inspect and adapt. Do not drop events "to save time".
  6. Only the Product Owner cancels a Sprint, and only if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Being behind is not a reason.
  7. Shorter Sprints limit risk and generate more learning. Choose them when uncertainty or change is high.
  8. The Sprint Goal and quality are protected during the Sprint. Scope may be renegotiated; the goal and the Definition of Done are not.
  9. The Sprint is the container of the other events. Planning, Daily Scrums, Review and Retrospective happen within it.
  10. Refinement is not an event. It is an ongoing activity.
  11. "Ceremonies", "meetings" and "iterations" are not Guide words. The Guide uses events and Sprints.

9Exam Q&A

9.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1Two days before the end of the Sprint, the Developers realize that three items will not be finished. They ask to extend the Sprint by three days. What is the best answer?

  • AAgree, since the Developers decide how long the Sprint takes and know best how much time they still need to finish the three items properly
  • BAsk the Product Owner to approve a longer Sprint, because the Product Owner is accountable for the schedule
  • CExplain that Sprints are fixed length, and help the Developers and the Product Owner decide about the unfinished items
  • DCancel the Sprint and start a new one, so that the unfinished items can be planned again from scratch
Show the answer

Answer: C. Sprints are fixed-length events that create consistency, so a Sprint is not extended. The unfinished items do not meet the Definition of Done and return to the Product Backlog, and the Developers and the Product Owner can still renegotiate scope. Cancelling is only for an obsolete Sprint Goal.

S2A new team wants to hold a "Sprint 0" of four weeks to set up the environment and gather all requirements before the first Sprint. How should the Scrum Master respond?

  • AExplain that all necessary work happens within Sprints, and help the team start with a first Sprint that delivers a small Increment
  • BAgree, because preparation of the environment and the requirements is part of Scrum and happens before the first Sprint, and the Product Owner signs off the requirements at its end
  • CExplain that Scrum requires the first Sprint to be exactly two weeks long, so a four-week Sprint 0 is not permitted
  • DAgree, as long as the Sprint 0 is shorter than one month and ends with a signed requirements document
Show the answer

Answer: A. The Guide places all the necessary work, including events, within Sprints, and Sprints are of one month or less and start one after another. A separate preparation phase is not part of Scrum. The Scrum Master helps the team start small. The Guide does not require two weeks.

S3Management wants the team to skip the Sprint Retrospective and the Sprint Review in the coming Sprint "to save time for coding". What should the Scrum Master do?

  • AAgree for one Sprint, because the team can recover the lost time and resume the events in the following Sprint, when the delivery pressure has eased
  • BAllow the team to decide event by event whether the time spent on it is worth the value that it brings
  • CReplace both events with an email summary sent to the stakeholders, so that they still receive the information
  • DExplain that skipping an event loses a chance to inspect and adapt, and help management see the value of both
Show the answer

Answer: D. Events are formal opportunities to inspect and adapt and they replace other meetings. Skipping them loses the feedback and the improvements that protect the Increment's quality and value. The Scrum Master helps the organization understand Scrum.

S4When should the Sprint Retrospective take place in the Sprint?

  • ABefore Sprint Planning of the same Sprint
  • BAt the end of the Sprint, after the Sprint Review, where it concludes the Sprint
  • CBefore the Sprint Review
  • DIn the middle of the Sprint
Show the answer

Answer: B. The Sprint Review is the second to last event and the Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint. This lets the team plan improvements for the next Sprint after inspecting the whole Sprint.

S5Halfway through the Sprint, the Developers conclude that the work is harder than expected and that the Sprint Goal may be missed. What is the best action?

  • AAsk the Scrum Master to cancel the Sprint, because the Sprint Goal can no longer be reached in the time left
  • BExtend the Sprint by a few days so that the Developers can finish all the planned work at the same quality
  • CLower the Definition of Done for the harder items so that they can still be finished within the original Sprint timebox
  • DCollaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog without affecting the Sprint Goal
Show the answer

Answer: D. A Sprint can be cancelled only if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, and only by the Product Owner. When work turns out different, the Developers and the Product Owner negotiate scope within the Sprint. Quality does not decrease and the Sprint is not extended.

S6Which set of maximum timeboxes is correct for a one-month Sprint?

  • APlanning 4 hours, Daily Scrum 15 minutes, Review 8 hours, Retrospective 3 hours
  • BPlanning 8 hours, Daily Scrum 15 minutes, Review 4 hours, Retrospective 3 hours
  • CPlanning 8 hours, Daily Scrum 30 minutes, Review 4 hours, Retrospective 4 hours
  • DPlanning 2 hours, Daily Scrum 15 minutes, Review 1 hour, Retrospective 1 hour
Show the answer

Answer: B. For a one-month Sprint the Guide sets a maximum of eight hours for Sprint Planning, 15 minutes for the Daily Scrum, four hours for the Sprint Review and three hours for the Sprint Retrospective. For shorter Sprints the other events are usually shorter.

S7A team works in a fast-changing market with high uncertainty and releases rarely. Which Sprint length best fits the Guide's reasoning?

  • ASix weeks, so that the team has more time in each Sprint to complete the large and complex items of the product
  • BTwo months, to reduce the number of events and the time that the team spends on planning and reviews
  • CA shorter Sprint, as long as a usable Increment fits in it, to generate more learning cycles and limit risk
  • DA Sprint length that changes from day to day, depending on how much the market has moved since the last day
Show the answer

Answer: C. The Guide says that a Sprint horizon that is too long may make the Sprint Goal invalid and increase complexity and risk, and that shorter Sprints generate more learning cycles. Sprints longer than one month are not allowed, and a length that varies removes consistency.

S8A team holds Sprint Planning on Monday, the Daily Scrum at changing times and places, and the Retrospective whenever the room is free. What does the Guide suggest?

  • AHold all events at the same time and place to reduce complexity, as far as possible
  • BHold each event in a different place to keep people alert
  • CLet the Scrum Master decide the schedule each week
  • DLet the Product Owner set all event times
Show the answer

Answer: A. Optimally, all events are held at the same time and place to reduce complexity. Regularity is one reason for events. The Scrum Master ensures that events take place; no one else needs to set the schedule each time.

S9A department head says: "Our product is complex, so we need six-week Sprints." What is the best response?

  • AAgree: complex work needs more time per Sprint, so a six-week Sprint is the right adaptation for a complex product
  • BAgree, but with a longer Sprint Planning so that the team can plan the additional weeks of work properly
  • CAgree if the Product Owner approves the longer Sprint after consulting the stakeholders and the Scrum Master
  • DExplain that Sprints are one month or less, because a longer horizon can invalidate the Sprint Goal and raise risk
Show the answer

Answer: D. The Sprint is a fixed-length event of one month or less. Complexity is a reason for shorter Sprints, not longer ones, because each Sprint inspects and adapts progress toward the Product Goal.

S10At the Daily Scrum, the Developers see that an item will take longer than planned, and they change the plan for the next day. Which statement describes this?

  • AThe Developers cancel the Sprint Backlog
  • BThe Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog
  • CThe Developers renegotiate the Sprint Goal with the stakeholders
  • DThe Developers change the Definition of Done for the Sprint
Show the answer

Answer: B. The purpose of the Daily Scrum is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary, adjusting the upcoming planned work. The Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done are not changed.

9.2 Recall Q&As

R1What is the Sprint?

Show the answer

A fixed-length event of one month or less that is the container for all other events; the heartbeat of Scrum, where ideas are turned into value.

R2What are the five Scrum events?

Show the answer

The Sprint (the container), Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective.

R3What starts when a Sprint ends?

Show the answer

The next Sprint, immediately.

R4What is each event?

Show the answer

A formal opportunity to inspect and adapt Scrum artifacts.

R5What happens when an event is not operated as prescribed?

Show the answer

Opportunities to inspect and adapt are lost.

R6Give the maximum timeboxes for a one-month Sprint.

Show the answer

Sprint Planning 8 hours; Daily Scrum 15 minutes; Sprint Review 4 hours; Sprint Retrospective 3 hours.

R7Which event is second to last, and which concludes the Sprint?

Show the answer

The Sprint Review is second to last; the Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint.

R8What are the rules during the Sprint?

Show the answer

No changes that would endanger the Sprint Goal; quality does not decrease; the Product Backlog is refined as needed; scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner.

R9Why can a Sprint horizon that is too long be a problem?

Show the answer

The Sprint Goal may become invalid, complexity may rise and risk may increase.

R10Name at least three benefits of a timebox.

Show the answer

Regularity and predictability; focus; faster decisions; limited waste and risk; a regular rhythm of inspection and adaptation; fewer unplanned meetings.

R11Name three factors in choosing a Sprint length.

Show the answer

How fast feedback is needed or the market changes; uncertainty and risk; how long a usable Increment takes; stakeholder availability. The maximum is one month.

R12When can a Sprint be cancelled, and by whom?

Show the answer

If the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, and only by the Product Owner.

R13At which pace should the events be held?

Show the answer

Optimally at the same time and place, to reduce complexity.

R14What is the Daily Scrum timebox in a two-week Sprint?

Show the answer

15 minutes, as in every Sprint.

10Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Sprint Fixed length, one month or less; container for all events; next Sprint starts immediately
Events 5: Sprint + Planning + Daily Scrum + Review + Retrospective
Each event A formal opportunity to inspect and adapt; skipping one loses it
Timeboxes (1-month Sprint) Planning 8 h · Daily Scrum 15 min · Review 4 h · Retrospective 3 h
Shorter Sprints Planning, Review and Retrospective usually shorter; Daily Scrum still 15 min
Sequence Planning → Daily Scrums + work → Review (second to last) → Retrospective (concludes)
During the Sprint No change that endangers the Sprint Goal · quality does not decrease · refine as needed · renegotiate scope
Sprint length One month or less; shorter limits risk and gives more learning; fixed
Timebox benefits Regularity · focus · faster decisions · limited risk · rhythm of inspection · fewer meetings
Cancel Product Owner only, if the Sprint Goal is obsolete
Not Scrum Sprint 0, hardening or release Sprint, extending a Sprint
Old wording "Ceremonies", 2017 cancellation detail
